# How are the three supporting tissues different?

<!-- STEP id="parenchyma" -->
## Parenchyma: soft and living
Parenchyma is made of living cells with thin walls. The cells are loosely packed, with intercellular spaces between them. Parenchyma mainly stores food, as in a potato, and in the green parts of a plant it also makes food by photosynthesis.

<!-- STEP id="air" -->
## Air spaces for floating
In aquatic plants such as lotus and water hyacinth, special parenchyma forms large air spaces. The air in these spaces helps the plants float.

<!-- STEP id="collenchyma" -->
## Collenchyma: thick at the corners
Collenchyma is made of living cells whose walls are thickened unevenly at the corners. The thickening is due to pectin, a substance that makes the walls flexible, like rubber. Collenchyma gives support and lets parts such as stems and tendrils bend without breaking.

<!-- STEP id="sclerenchyma" -->
## Sclerenchyma: hard and mostly dead
Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls, because a substance called lignin is laid down in them. Lignin makes the walls hard and strong, and forms the woody parts of a plant. Most of these cells are dead. Sclerenchyma is found in stems, in leaf veins, and in the hard coverings of seeds and nuts, such as coconut husk and walnut shell.

<!-- STEP id="bend" -->
## The bend test
A fresh twig curves when you bend it. Its cells are living and full of water, and flexible tissue such as collenchyma lets it bend. A dry twig has lost its water, so what is left is mostly stiff, dry cell walls, and it snaps.

**Parenchyma is soft, collenchyma bends, and sclerenchyma stays hard.**
